prompt: A free-response question shows partial regression output for predicting a car's fuel economy (mpg) from its weight (hundreds of kg): the slope is $b = -0.45$ and its $t$ statistic for testing $H_0: \beta = 0$ is $t = -2.5$. The standard error of the slope is missing from the output. What is $SE_b$?
hint: The $t$ statistic in the output was built from the slope and its standard error. You know two of those three numbers, so work backward.

hints.text: The $t$ statistic in the output was built from the slope and its standard error. You know two of those three numbers, so work backward.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: if $b = 6$ and $t = 3$, then $6 / SE_b = 3$, so $SE_b = 2$. The algebra is the same here, but watch the negatives.
The statistic was computed as $t = \frac{b}{SE_b}$, so write $-2.5 = \frac{-0.45}{SE_b}$ and rearrange it to $SE_b = \frac{-0.45}{-2.5}$.
$0.45 / 2.5 = 0.18$, so the standard error of the slope is $0.18$ mpg per hundred kg.

explanation: The $t$ statistic for a slope is $t = b / SE_b$ when the null value is 0.
Rearranging to isolate the unknown gives $SE_b = b / t = (-0.45)/(-2.5)$.
$SE_b = 0.18$. Standard errors are always positive, which the two negatives confirm. (A $95\%$ interval would be roughly $-0.45 \pm t^*(0.18)$.)

alternativeExplanations.title: Check it forwards
steps: Reading output backwards like this is a common free-response move: the test always links $b$, $SE_b$ and $t$.
Any one of the three can be recovered from the other two.
